snippet.title: The Gillette Family: From Utopian Socialists to Dying Broke
snippet.description:
In January 2005, Procter & Gamble purchased the Gillette Company for $57 billion — one of the largest consumer goods acquisitions in history, anchoring a brand today valued at approximately $14.5 billion. The face on those billions of razor blade wrappers belonged to King Camp Gillette, the man who invented the disposable economy, designed the razor-and-blade business model that would later govern every printer cartridge and coffee pod on Earth, and died on July 9, 1932, in Los Angeles nearly bankrupt — his stock devoured by the Depression, his company taken from him by investors, his only son destined to die childless in 1955 and end the direct family line. He had also spent his entire adult life writing utopian manifestos arguing that capitalism was the root cause of human misery, offered Theodore Roosevelt $1 million to lead a global socialist corporation, collaborated with Upton Sinclair on a blueprint for abolishing the profit motive, and designed a porcelain-clad megacity called Metropolis that would house the entire American population powered by Niagara Falls — all while building one of the most ruthlessly profitable consumer brands of the twentieth century.

———————————————————

Gain FREE access to secret full-length documentaries on wealthy families "too scandalous for YouTube" by joining our newsletter: https://www.substack.com/@oldmoneyluxury

———————————————————

The Gillette family's American story begins with the St. Bartholomew's Day Massacre of August 24, 1572 — when Reverend Jacques de Gylet, a Huguenot minister in Bergerac, escaped the slaughter of French Protestants, fled to Scotland and then England, and watched his property in Bergerac be confiscated.

His grandsons, Jonathan and Nathan, crossed the Atlantic in 1630 on the ship John and Mary, settling at Windsor, Connecticut, and the family spread for two centuries through New England and the old Northwest Territory as farmers, ministers, and occasional tradesmen.

King Camp Gillette was born on January 5, 1855, in Fond du Lac, Wisconsin, to George Wolcott Gillette — a tinkering postmaster and newspaper editor — and Fanny Lemira Camp, whose 1887 cookbook "The White House Cook Book" became one of the best-selling cookbooks in American history and remains in print to this day.

The family hardware business was destroyed in the Great Chicago Fire of 1871 — a formative catastrophe that pushed King onto the road as a traveling salesman for the Crown Cork & Seal Company, working under William Painter, the inventor of the disposable bottle cap.

In 1891, Painter gave King the advice that would define his life: invent something that is used, thrown away, and replaced — and in 1895, while shaving with a dulled straight razor at a hotel mirror in Brookline, Massachusetts, King conceived the disposable safety razor blade.

It took six years of laboratory work and a partnership with MIT machinist William Nickerson before the Gillette Safety Razor Company was incorporated in 1901 above a fish shop in Boston — and within two decades, Gillette had become one of the most profitable consumer brands in American history, with its founder's face appearing on every blade wrapper shipped worldwide.

Simultaneously, King published four major utopian manifestos arguing that competition was "the root of all evil," that competitive waste consumed the majority of all human productive energy, and that the solution was the "United Company" — a single publicly owned mega-corporation that would absorb every industry on Earth and distribute profits equally to every citizen.

He offered Theodore Roosevelt $1 million to lead a global socialist corporation, collaborated with Upton Sinclair on a blueprint for abolishing the profit motive, and designed a city called Metropolis that would house 60 million Americans in porcelain-clad towers powered by Niagara Falls, connected by transparent sidewalks designed to make the labor sustaining civilization permanently visible.

He described the contradiction himself in a letter to Sinclair: "My life seemed to separate into two distinct entities, one devoted to earning a living and the other to the problem of how to overcome the difficulties of the industrial world" — calling himself "a man with two souls."

In the 1920s, with Gillette stock trading at $125 a share, King built a 588-acre estate in Calabasas, California, and lived as one of the wealthiest men in the American West — but he was simultaneously losing control of the company to investors and bankers, outmaneuvered through a combination of patent warfare, possible industrial espionage, and a disclosure of financial irregularities that sent the stock into freefall at the worst possible moment in American economic history.

snippet.title: The $23 Billion Family That Secretly Built the Iraq Invasion You Never Heard Of: The Bechtels
snippet.description:
They built the Hoover Dam. They paved the bones of Saudi Arabia from scratch on 20,000 workers a month for half a century. They managed the cleanup of Three Mile Island and Chernobyl, bored the Channel Tunnel, oversaw the reconstruction of Iraq twice, and built the world's first electricity-producing nuclear reactor in 1949. They have been involved in more than 25,000 projects across 160 countries since 1898 — and have provided to the United States government, at various points, the Director of the CIA, the Secretary of State, the Secretary of Defense, the Deputy Secretary of Energy, members of the Pentagon's Defense Policy Board, and a special envoy sent to Baghdad in 1983 to pitch Saddam Hussein on a $2 billion pipeline. Ask the average American who the Bechtels are, and they will draw a blank. That blank is not an accident. It is a strategic choice, cultivated across five generations, that has insulated one of the most consequential privately held corporations in American history from the public scrutiny that ordinary business empires attract.

———————————————————

Gain FREE access to secret full-length documentaries on wealthy families "too scandalous for YouTube" by joining our newsletter: https://www.substack.com/@oldmoneyluxury

———————————————————

Warren A. Bechtel left a Kansas farm with a team of mules in 1898 to grade railroad track beds in the Oklahoma Territory for $2.75 a day — and within three decades had built one of the largest construction firms in the American West.

In 1931, Warren led the consortium of six companies known as Six Companies, Inc. that won the contract to build the Hoover Dam — at the time the largest construction project in American history — and Bechtel emerged from the Depression as one of the most powerful contractors on Earth.

Warren died unexpectedly in 1933, and his son Stephen Davison Bechtel Sr. took over the company at age 32 — pivoting the firm into the pipeline business with the Trans-Arabian Pipeline of the 1940s, the construction of the petroleum infrastructure of Saudi Arabia from scratch, and a partnership with the House of Saud that has now lasted more than 80 years.

In 1949, Bechtel built the world's first electricity-producing nuclear reactor — the EBR-I in Idaho — establishing the company as the dominant private contractor in the American nuclear program for the next four decades.

John A. McCone, a Bechtel co-founder of the California Shipbuilding Corporation during World War II, walked from the firm's orbit directly into the directorship of the Central Intelligence Agency under President Kennedy in 1961 — establishing the executive-pipeline pattern that would define the family's relationship to American government for the next half-century.

Stephen Davison Bechtel Jr. took the company global in the 1960s and 1970s, executing the Jubail industrial city project in Saudi Arabia — one of the largest civil-engineering projects in human history, employing 40,000 workers at its peak — and overseeing the build-out of the kingdom's modern infrastructure on a scale unmatched by any other private contractor.

George P. Shultz served as Bechtel's president from 1975 until he was appointed Secretary of State by Ronald Reagan in 1982 — and Caspar Weinberger served as Bechtel's general counsel before being appointed Reagan's Secretary of Defense the same year.

In 1983, Donald Rumsfeld traveled to Baghdad as a special envoy to meet Saddam Hussein — a trip whose agenda included a proposed $2 billion oil pipeline that Bechtel was positioned to build across Jordan to the port of Aqaba.

Bechtel managed the cleanup of Three Mile Island after the 1979 partial meltdown, advised on the response to Chernobyl, and was the lead contractor on Boston's "Big Dig" — the most expensive highway project in American history, plagued by cost overruns, structural failures, and litigation that consumed two decades.

In 1999, Bechtel's subsidiary in Cochabamba, Bolivia, became the focus of one of the most consequential anti-privatization uprisings in Latin American history — the Cochabamba Water War — after rate increases following the privatization of the city's water system triggered mass protests that left several dead and forced the contract's cancellation.

In 2003, Bechtel was awarded the first major reconstruction contract in postwar Iraq — a $680 million no-bid contract from USAID, expanded to more than $2.3 billion across multiple projects — making the company the single largest private beneficiary of the American reconstruction program in the country.

Riley Bechtel led the firm through the exposed decade of the 2000s, and the company has since been handed to Brendan Bechtel — the fifth generation of the family, a Stanford-educated chief executive who speaks the contemporary language of clean energy, sustainability, and ethical conduct.

snippet.description:
This in-depth, full-length documentary tells the story of the Mellon dynasty — the Ulster Scots Pittsburgh banking family who financed other people's furnaces, oil drillers, and aluminum smelters until they controlled Gulf Oil, Alcoa, Koppers, Carborundum, and Mellon National Bank, paid more federal income tax than anyone alive except John D. Rockefeller and Henry Ford, served three sitting Presidents as Secretary of the Treasury, donated the National Gallery of Art to the United States, and on a per-capita basis briefly became richer than the Rockefellers themselves.

---------------------

Gain FREE access to secret full-length documentaries on wealthy families "too scandalous for YouTube" by joining our newsletter: https://www.substack.com/@oldmoneyluxury

---------------------

Thomas Mellon was born in 1813 in County Tyrone, Ireland, emigrated to western Pennsylvania at age five, and at fourteen read Benjamin Franklin's autobiography and resolved to leave farming for the city.

In 1869, at age 56, the former judge opened T. Mellon and Sons on Smithfield Street in Pittsburgh, with a near-life-size statue of Benjamin Franklin above the door and his two eldest sons already inside. Within two decades it was the largest private bank between New York and Chicago.

The youngest son, Andrew William Mellon, took over the firm in 1882 at twenty-seven and proceeded to finance the four engines of the family fortune — Gulf Oil, Alcoa, Koppers, and Carborundum — by lending against industries his rivals did not yet understand.

In 1921 Andrew Mellon was appointed Secretary of the Treasury by President Warren Harding and remained in the post under Coolidge and Hoover, an eleven-year tenure during which the press joked that "three Presidents served under him."

In 1932, in the depths of the Depression, the Roosevelt administration brought tax fraud charges against him; he was acquitted by a federal grand jury but died in 1937 having quietly donated his art collection and 15 million dollars to build the National Gallery of Art in Washington as a gift to the United States.

By 1957, Fortune's first comprehensive ranking of richest Americans placed four members of one family — Paul, Ailsa, Sarah, and Richard King Mellon — in the top eight, each worth between 400 and 700 million dollars, briefly making the descendants of the Franklin statue richer per capita than the descendants of John D. Rockefeller.

This is the story of how a Tyrone-born judge built a Pittsburgh dynasty that quietly financed the industrial revolution of the United States, ruled the American Treasury for eleven years, and gave the country its greatest art museum — while remaining the most reserved and least understood of the great Gilded Age families.

snippet.title: The $2 Billion Grocery Heir Who Died Broke on His Private Island: Huntington Hartford
snippet.description:
In this in-depth, full-length documentary, we explore the life of Huntington Hartford — heir to the A&P grocery fortune who inherited approximately $100 million, owned 10 percent of the largest retailer in the world, was paid $1.5 million a year from a trust beginning at age six, and across seventy-five years spent close to $1 billion in 2008 dollars on a Manhattan museum the critics destroyed, a Bahamas private island he developed without a casino license, an artists' colony, a magazine, a Broadway flop, four marriages, and a long late chapter of cocaine, Quaaludes, and tendons slashed by his own household.

----------------------------------------

Gain FREE access to secret full-length documentaries on wealthy families "too scandalous for YouTube" by joining our newsletter: https://www.substack.com/@oldmoneyluxury

----------------------------------------

George Huntington Hartford II was born April 18, 1911 in New York City — second of two children of Edward V. Hartford, the inventor of the automobile shock absorber, and Henrietta Guerard Pollitzer Hartford. His grandfather had founded the Great American Tea Company at 31 Vesey Street in 1859, renamed it the Great Atlantic and Pacific Tea Company in 1869 in honor of the just-completed transcontinental railroad, and built it into a chain that by 1930 operated 16,000 stores in 39 states with $2.9 billion in sales — the largest retailer in the world.

Edward died in 1922 when Huntington was eleven, refusing medical treatment as a Christian Scientist. The trust began paying Huntington $1.5 million per year. His mother Henrietta — vain, beautiful, "very domineering" in his own later words — moved the family to the Seaverge estate in Newport next to Doris Duke's Rough Point and cut his teenage meat at dinner parties. In 1934, his uncles tried him in the A&P statistics department; he chose the Harvard-Yale football game over reporting to work and was cut from management forever.

He eloped with dentist's daughter Mary Lee Epling at 20, refusing his mother's preferred match with Doris Duke. He bought the square-rigger Joseph Conrad in 1936 from Australian sailor Alan Villiers and used her as a private yacht before donating her to the U.S. Maritime Commission in 1939; she survives at Mystic Seaport.

In 1949 at Ciro's on the Sunset Strip, Hartford bought all the cigarettes from 18-year-old cigarette girl Marjorie Steele. Charlie Chaplin told his son Sydney to step aside because Hartford had more money. Marjorie organized his most productive decade — the Huntington Hartford Foundation artists' colony in Rustic Canyon (more than 400 residencies including Edward Hopper and Ernst Toch), the Huntington Hartford Theatre on Vine Street, the figurative art collection that became the centerpiece of his museum.

In 1956 he bought the lot at the south end of Columbus Circle for nearly $1 million. Edward Durell Stone designed the nine-story marble-clad Gallery of Modern Art with a concave facade and a colonnade Ada Louise Huxtable in The New York Times called "a die-cut Venetian palazzo on lollipops." The building cost $7.5 million. It opened March 21, 1964 with Salvador Dalí's commissioned The Discovery of America by Christopher Columbus on the wall and a $580,000 annual deficit on the books. Hartford had built it as a rebuttal to MoMA — his 1964 Doubleday book Art or Anarchy? called Picasso a "potentially great painter who never developed" and abstract expressionism "an ice age of art." His Show: The Magazine of the Arts, launched October 1961, lost $8 to $10 million across two runs. He transferred 2 Columbus Circle to Fairleigh Dickinson University in July 1969. Total loss: approximately $7.4 million.

In 1959 he bought four-fifths of Hog Island in the Bahamas from Axel Wenner-Gren — the Electrolux founder placed on the U.S. Proclaimed List of Blocked Nationals in 1942 — for $9 to $11 million. He renamed it Paradise Island in 1962, built the 52-room Ocean Club, reassembled a 14th-century French Augustinian monastery William Randolph Hearst had stored in a Florida warehouse, hired Gary Player as golf pro and Pancho Gonzales as tennis pro, and threw the Bal du Paradis on February 17, 1962 with 2,000 guests, fireworks from Monaco, and the Beatles filming Help! on the beach. He had not negotiated a casino license. Sir Stafford Sands, behind whom stood Meyer Lansky, would not grant one unless Hartford surrendered the island. He sold to the Mary Carter Paint Company in January 1966 for an effective payment as low as $1 million on an investment of $25-30 million. Mary Carter renamed itself Resorts International, opened the Paradise Island Casino in 1968, and in 1978 opened the first legal casino in Atlantic City.

In this in-depth, full-length documentary, we explore the life of Huntington Hartford — heir to the A&P grocery fortune who inherited approximately $100 million, owned 10 percent of the largest retailer in the world, was paid $1.5 million a year from a trust beginning at age six, and across seventy-five years spent close to $1 billion in 2008 dollars on a Manhattan museum the critics destroyed, a Bahamas private island he developed without a casino license, an artists' colony, a magazine, a Broadway flop, four marriages, and a long late chapter of cocaine, Quaaludes, and tendons slashed by his own household.

----------------------------------------

Gain FREE access to secret full-length documentaries on wealthy families "too scandalous for YouTube" by joining our newsletter: https://www.substack.com/@oldmoneyluxury

----------------------------------------

George Huntington Hartford II was born April 18, 1911 in New York City — second of two children of Edward V. Hartford, the inventor of the automobile shock absorber, and Henrietta Guerard Pollitzer Hartford. His grandfather had founded the Great American Tea Company at 31 Vesey Street in 1859, renamed it the Great Atlantic and Pacific Tea Company in 1869 in honor of the just-completed transcontinental railroad, and built it into a chain that by 1930 operated 16,000 stores in 39 states with $2.9 billion in sales — the largest retailer in the world.

Edward died in 1922 when Huntington was eleven, refusing medical treatment as a Christian Scientist. The trust began paying Huntington $1.5 million per year. His mother Henrietta — vain, beautiful, "very domineering" in his own later words — moved the family to the Seaverge estate in Newport next to Doris Duke's Rough Point and cut his teenage meat at dinner parties. In 1934, his uncles tried him in the A&P statistics department; he chose the Harvard-Yale football game over reporting to work and was cut from management forever.

He eloped with dentist's daughter Mary Lee Epling at 20, refusing his mother's preferred match with Doris Duke. He bought the square-rigger Joseph Conrad in 1936 from Australian sailor Alan Villiers and used her as a private yacht before donating her to the U.S. Maritime Commission in 1939; she survives at Mystic Seaport.

In 1949 at Ciro's on the Sunset Strip, Hartford bought all the cigarettes from 18-year-old cigarette girl Marjorie Steele. Charlie Chaplin told his son Sydney to step aside because Hartford had more money. Marjorie organized his most productive decade — the Huntington Hartford Foundation artists' colony in Rustic Canyon (more than 400 residencies including Edward Hopper and Ernst Toch), the Huntington Hartford Theatre on Vine Street, the figurative art collection that became the centerpiece of his museum.

In 1956 he bought the lot at the south end of Columbus Circle for nearly $1 million. Edward Durell Stone designed the nine-story marble-clad Gallery of Modern Art with a concave facade and a colonnade Ada Louise Huxtable in The New York Times called "a die-cut Venetian palazzo on lollipops." The building cost $7.5 million. It opened March 21, 1964 with Salvador Dalí's commissioned The Discovery of America by Christopher Columbus on the wall and a $580,000 annual deficit on the books. Hartford had built it as a rebuttal to MoMA — his 1964 Doubleday book Art or Anarchy? called Picasso a "potentially great painter who never developed" and abstract expressionism "an ice age of art." His Show: The Magazine of the Arts, launched October 1961, lost $8 to $10 million across two runs. He transferred 2 Columbus Circle to Fairleigh Dickinson University in July 1969. Total loss: approximately $7.4 million.

In 1959 he bought four-fifths of Hog Island in the Bahamas from Axel Wenner-Gren — the Electrolux founder placed on the U.S. Proclaimed List of Blocked Nationals in 1942 — for $9 to $11 million. He renamed it Paradise Island in 1962, built the 52-room Ocean Club, reassembled a 14th-century French Augustinian monastery William Randolph Hearst had stored in a Florida warehouse, hired Gary Player as golf pro and Pancho Gonzales as tennis pro, and threw the Bal du Paradis on February 17, 1962 with 2,000 guests, fireworks from Monaco, and the Beatles filming Help! on the beach. He had not negotiated a casino license. Sir Stafford Sands, behind whom stood Meyer Lansky, would not grant one unless Hartford surrendered the island. He sold to the Mary Carter Paint Company in January 1966 for an effective payment as low as $1 million on an investment of $25-30 million. Mary Carter renamed itself Resorts International, opened the Paradise Island Casino in 1968, and in 1978 opened the first legal casino in Atlantic City.

snippet.title: The Firefighter Brothers Who Started With $100 and Sold for $1 Billion in Cash: Firehouse Subs
snippet.description:
When Chris and Robin Sorensen opened the first Firehouse Subs on October 10, 1994, in a strip mall in Jacksonville, Florida, they had less than a hundred dollars left in their personal checking accounts. The first day's receipts amounted to little more than "two hot dogs" — company lore's shorthand for a launch nobody noticed. Twenty-seven years later, Restaurant Brands International — the global parent of Burger King, Tim Hortons, and Popeyes — paid one billion dollars in all cash to own what they built.

-------------------

Gain FREE access to secret full-length documentaries on wealthy families "too scandalous for YouTube" by joining our newsletter: https://www.substack.com/@oldmoneyluxury

-------------------

The Sorensen brothers grew up in Jacksonville in a household steeped in the fire service — their father, Rob, served more than four decades in the Jacksonville Fire and Rescue Department. Both sons followed him into public safety careers before opening a sub shop in 1994.

Before Firehouse, every business venture they had tried had failed. By the time the first store opened, they had no cushion at home. Chris kept working firefighter shifts without drawing a paycheck. Robin's salary from the restaurant hovered at $12,000 to $15,000 a year for nearly a decade.

The first attempt at franchising came in 1995, barely a year after opening. The brothers quickly realized they were not ready and made one of the most revealing decisions in the brand's history — they halted franchising and bought back their own units to protect brand integrity.

Around 2001, they relaunched with proper training programs, manuals, and selection criteria. By 2010, the chain had grown to 379 locations. By July 2016, they had opened the thousandth restaurant.

In 2005, after feeding first responders on the Gulf Coast in the aftermath of Hurricane Katrina, the founders created the Firehouse Subs Public Safety Foundation — distributing defibrillators, fire trucks, radios, and turnout gear to small departments that could not afford them. By the time of the acquisition, it had granted $62.5 million. The cumulative total has since passed $100 million.

When RBI announced the $1 billion all-cash deal in November 2021, the system had roughly 1,200 restaurants generating about $1.1 billion in system-wide sales and $50 million of adjusted EBITDA — meaning RBI paid roughly twenty times earnings for a brand whose deepest asset was not unit economics but emotional loyalty no competitor could replicate.

-------------------

Today the system has grown past 1,400 locations under RBI, and Chris and Robin remain the public faces of the founding story — two firefighters who started with less than a hundred dollars and proved that authenticity, patience, and the willingness to admit you are not ready compound over decades.

snippet.title: The Pabst Beer Dynasty: Prohibition, a Haunted Mansion, and the Blue Ribbon That Was Never Real
snippet.description:
In June 1893, the Adams Express Company delivered a wooden crate to the Agricultural Building at the World's Columbian Exposition in Chicago. Inside was a scale model of a Milwaukee brewery, 13 square feet across, cast in gold-washed bronze and white metal. It had cost approximately $100,000 to make — the equivalent of several million dollars in today's money. The man who had ordered it was a former Great Lakes steamship captain named Frederick Pabst, the president of what was about to become the largest brewery on earth. The gold brewery sat at the center of his pavilion for six months, watched by 27 million fair-goers. The competition the model was meant to celebrate would end in chaos, with judges accused of clerical error, a beer baron's lawyers dispatched to Europe to hunt down a witness, and two rival breweries claiming the same victory. The blue ribbons that would eventually wrap themselves around the entire mythology had nothing to do with that fair.

In this in-depth episode of Old Money Luxury, we trace six generations of the Pabst Beer Dynasty — from a Great Lakes steamship captain who married the boss's daughter, to the largest brewery in the world, to a Flemish Renaissance castle in Milwaukee, to a Prohibition survival plan built on processed cheese and motorcycle floor space, to a modern virtual brewer that owns a legend and contracts out the beer.

-------------------

Gain FREE access to secret full-length documentaries on wealthy families "too scandalous for YouTube" by joining our newsletter: https://www.substack.com/@oldmoneyluxury

-------------------

We open on Lake Michigan in the 1850s — Captain Frederick Pabst on the wheelhouse of Great Lakes side-wheel steamers, the 1862 collision that wrecked the Sea Bird off Whitefish Point, and the maritime career that ended the day a young steamboat captain married Maria Best, daughter of Milwaukee brewer Phillip Best.

We follow Frederick out of the wheelhouse and into the Empire Brewery in 1864 — the partnership with his father-in-law, the buyout of the Best interests, and the transformation of a middle-tier Milwaukee brewery into the industrial engine that would define the American lager market.

We trace the technical revolution — Louis Pasteur's brewing research at the École normale in Paris, the first commercial pasteurization line for beer, the mechanical refrigeration that broke the seasonal ceiling, and the rail-refrigerator network that carried Milwaukee lager to every corner of the continent.

We watch Frederick Pabst overtake Anheuser-Busch in 1889 as the largest brewery on earth — the first American brewery to exceed one million barrels a year, the vertical integration into cooperage, malt houses, and its own rail fleet, and the operating culture that separated Pabst from every regional competitor in the country.

We reconstruct the "Blue Ribbon" — the actual satin ribbons that Pabst tied around the neck of every bottle beginning in 1882, the 300,000 yards of silk consumed each year, and the marketing artifact that would only be retroactively re-attributed to a fair that had never awarded such a thing.

We walk through the 1893 World's Columbian Exposition — the gold-washed brewery model, the six-month White City, the scoring dispute with Anheuser-Busch, the lawyers sent to Europe to depose the vanishing judge, and the phrase "Selected as America's Best in 1893" that would be quietly grafted onto the label in the 1950s by a marketing team that needed a story.

We tour the Flemish Renaissance mansion at 2000 West Wisconsin Avenue — Ferdinand Ringoffer's iron work, the domestic chapel, the servants' wing, and the Milwaukee palace the Great Lakes captain built in stone at the peak of his empire.

We follow Frederick's death in 1904, the succession of Gustav and Fred Jr., and the sober generation that carried Pabst into the collision that no brewer in America saw coming: the Eighteenth Amendment.

We reconstruct the Prohibition survival strategy — Pabst-ett processed cheese produced under a Kraft licensing arrangement, Pablo near-beer, the malt syrup, the industrial soft drinks, the motorcycle-storage business inside the empty warehouses, and the artichoke import subsidiary that kept the ledger black across 13 dry years.

We follow the post-Prohibition recovery, the mid-century peak, the merger, and the long generational decline of the third and fourth Pabst heirs — the deaths, the divorces, the boardroom fights, and the slow surrender of operating control by a family that had grown out of the plant.

We trace the 1985 sale to Kalmanovitz and the collapse of the corporate empire — the closing of the historic Milwaukee brewery, the migration to contract production, and the 1975 preservation fight that saved the Flemish castle at 2000 West Wisconsin from becoming a parking lot.

snippet.description:
#GrosvenorFamily #OldMoneyDynasties #LondonBillionaires

For more than three centuries, one extraordinary dynasty has quietly shaped the heart of London. This is the untold story of the Grosvenor family, the old money empire that turned forgotten marshland into some of the most valuable real estate on Earth. From Mayfair to Belgravia, from private palaces to international luxury districts, the Grosvenors built a fortune unlike anything the modern world has ever seen.

In this documentary, we uncover how a single marriage in 1677 ignited a multi-billion dollar legacy, how the family crafted a genius leasing strategy that ensured wealth would never leave their hands, and how their influence expanded across continents through strategic vision, global investments, and unbreakable legal structures.

Today, the Grosvenors stand as one of the most powerful dynasties in the world, with a global footprint stretching across Europe, North America, and Asia. But behind the luxury, the titles, and the centuries of privilege lies a story of strategy, controversy, survival, and transformation.

This is not just the story of a rich family. It is the story of a dynasty that built a city, protected an empire, and mastered the art of generational wealth. Watch as we reveal how the Grosvenors became the silent force behind London’s identity and how their influence continues to shape the world today.

snippet.title: How The Welch's Family Accidentally Built a $700 Million Empire
snippet.description:
In 1869, in the kitchen of a house in Vineland, New Jersey, a dentist named Thomas Bramwell Welch boiled twelve quart bottles of Concord grape juice on his stove, killed the yeast, and accidentally invented the entire American processed fruit juice industry. He was trying to keep alcohol off his church's communion table. Local pastors turned him down flat. By 1873 he had given up, gone back to selling dental alloys, and would die thirty years later without ever once mentioning the grape juice in his own autobiography. Today, Welch's generates close to $700 million a year, sells in more than 35 countries, and is owned collectively by roughly 670 family farmers — built, at every pivotal moment, entirely by accident.

In this in-depth episode of Old Money Luxury, we trace how a failed communion experiment in a New Jersey kitchen became one of the most recognized food brands in America — through a diplomatic scandal, a navy order, a constitutional amendment, two world wars, a molasses trader's tax problem, and a generation of soldiers who came home wanting grape jelly on their bread.

-------------------

Gain FREE access to secret full-length documentaries on wealthy families "too scandalous for YouTube" by joining our newsletter: https://www.substack.com/@oldmoneyluxury

-------------------

We open in the kitchen at Vineland in 1869 — twelve quart bottles, forty pounds of Concord grapes, cork and wax, and a dentist applying Pasteur's experiments to fresh fruit juice for the first time in history.

We meet Thomas Bramwell Welch — Underground Railroad conductor, Methodist minister, dentist, traveling physician, Philadelphia police officer sworn in to apprehend illegal liquor sellers — and the temperance utopia of Vineland, a planned town whose founding covenant banned alcohol.

We follow the collapse: pastors refusing the product on theological grounds, three years of small batches for a handful of churches, and Welch abandoning the project entirely by 1873 and going back to Welch's Dental Supply Company and Items of Interest magazine.

We watch his son Charles E. Welch resurrect the business in a shack behind the family home, rebrand "Dr. Welch's Unfermented Wine" to "Dr. Welch's Grape Juice," and turn a communion substitute into a household beverage by changing three words on a label.

We follow the move to Westfield, New York — the self-proclaimed "Grape Juice Capital of the World" — after black rot wiped out the Vineland vineyards in 1895, and the 1893 World's Columbian Exposition that turned a regional temperance product into a national brand overnight.

We reconstruct the 1913 diplomatic accident: Secretary of State William Jennings Bryan serving Welch's grape juice instead of wine at a state dinner for the British ambassador, the press storm that followed, and the Navy order from Josephus Daniels that turned a marketing scandal into a federal contract.

We trace Prohibition as a business plan — the 18th Amendment effectively eliminating Welch's only direct competitor — and the wartime jam, Grapelade, that the U.S. Army ordered for trench rations and that came home in the form of the peanut butter and jelly sandwich.

We meet Jack Kaplan, the molasses king who bought Welch's in 1945 and engineered the cooperative structure in 1956 — the company that bought itself, as a tax workaround that handed ownership to the 670 grape-growing families who still own it today.

We follow the television, lunchbox, and licensing era — the $700 million machine, the PIM Brands fruit-snack partnership, and the company's 2025 move into a new corporate headquarters in Waltham, Massachusetts.

And we close with Ephraim Wales Bull — the Massachusetts horticulturalist who bred the Concord grape from 22,000 seedlings, died poor because plant varieties were unpatentable, and whose gravestone — "He Sowed, Others Reaped" — could serve as the motto for every person who built the Welch's empire without ever capturing the value they created.

snippet.title: The Beer Dynasties That Drank Away Billions (Documentary)
snippet.description:
In this in-depth, full-length documentary, we explore the rise and fall of four of the most powerful family beer dynasties in modern history — the Strohs of Detroit, who turned a $9 billion fortune into bankruptcy in twenty years, the Anheuser-Busch family, who lost the King of Beers to InBev in 2008, the Uihleins of Schlitz, who built the most popular beer in America and watched it collapse from a single ingredient change, and the Heinekens of Amsterdam, the family that survived a 1983 kidnapping and is the only one of the four still in the chair.

---------------------------------

Gain FREE access to secret full-length documentaries on wealthy families "too scandalous for YouTube" by joining our newsletter: https://www.substack.com/@oldmoneyluxury

---------------------------------

In 1988, Forbes valued the Stroh family of Detroit at approximately $9 billion. By 2008, the Strohs had nothing left.

Bernhard Stroh had arrived from Kirn, Germany in 1850 with $150 in his pocket. He set up a beer plant on Catherine Street in Detroit and brewed the Bohemian-style lager his father had taught him. By the time Bernhard's grandson Peter Stroh died in 2002, the family had purchased Schaefer in 1981 and Schlitz in 1982, becoming the third-largest brewer in America in less than eighteen months.

The Schlitz acquisition was the bullet that killed them. The brand had already been destroyed by a chain of decisions made in the 1970s by Robert Uihlein Jr., the great-grandson of August Uihlein, the immigrant who had inherited Schlitz when his uncle Joseph Schlitz died in a shipwreck in 1875. To increase margins, Uihlein switched from real malt to corn syrup adjuncts and to a new "accelerated batch fermentation" process that cut brewing time in half. The beer began separating in the can. Customers called it the "snot beer." Schlitz collapsed from the most popular beer in America to a brand the Strohs paid $500 million to inherit at exactly the wrong moment.

The Strohs took on debt to compete with Anheuser-Busch and Miller and lost. By 1999, the family sold the breweries to Pabst and Miller for an amount that, after debt, left the heirs with effectively nothing.

Anheuser-Busch was older and lasted longer. Adolphus Busch, a German immigrant son of a hardware merchant, married Lilly Anheuser in 1861 and inherited the brewery from his father-in-law in 1865. He invented Budweiser in 1876 by stealing a recipe from a Bohemian town named Budweis. By the time he died in 1913, Anheuser-Busch was the largest brewery in America.

His great-grandson August Busch III ran the company through its modern peak — Bud Light, the Clydesdales, the Super Bowl ads. He fired his own son, August Busch IV, from the presidency twice. In 2008, the Belgian-Brazilian conglomerate InBev launched a $52 billion hostile takeover. August IV was the family member who signed the surrender. He sold for $70 a share. The deal closed in November 2008. The family received approximately $1.4 billion. The brewery has not been controlled by a Busch since.

Schlitz, before its collapse, had been the most popular beer in America from 1902 through the 1950s. Joseph Schlitz had inherited the brewery from August Krug in 1856 and married Krug's widow. When Schlitz drowned in the wreck of the SS Schiller off the Isles of Scilly in 1875, the brewery passed to his nephew August Uihlein. The Uihlein family ran Schlitz for ninety-six years and lost it in five.

Heineken is the only one of the four still standing. Gerard Heineken purchased a Haarlemmer brewery on Amsterdam's Rembrandtplein in 1864. His son Henry-Pierre patented the Heineken A-Yeast in 1886, the strain that gives the beer its consistent flavor across 192 countries. Henry-Pierre's grandson Freddy Heineken built the international empire. On November 9, 1983, Freddy was kidnapped at gunpoint outside the Amsterdam headquarters by a gang led by Cor van Hout and Willem Holleeder. He was held for three weeks in a soundproof cell in a warehouse in Diemen. The family paid a $35 million ransom. Freddy was released. He spent the rest of his life under armed protection. He died in 2002. His daughter Charlene de Carvalho-Heineken, with a personal net worth of approximately $20 billion, controls the company today.

Four dynasties, three collapses. The Heinekens survived because they kept the brewery in the family and refused to compete on volume. The Strohs, Schlitzes, and Buschs all died trying.

snippet.description:
Discover the dramatic story of the House of Wessex and the Saxon kings of England in this full-length historical documentary. This film explores how the early Anglo-Saxon kingdom of Wessex rose from a regional power to England’s first royal dynasty, shaping medieval England and the English monarchy itself.

Follow the lives of key figures such as Alfred the Great, Athelstan, Edward the Confessor and Harold Godwinson as they battle Viking invasions, rival Saxon kingdoms and internal power struggles. Through biography, warfare and politics, we trace the formation of early England from scattered Anglo-Saxon kingdoms to a united realm.

This House of Wessex documentary examines Viking raids, the Danelaw, the unification of England, the rise of Saxon kings, and the Norman Conquest that destroyed their dynasty at the Battle of Hastings. Packed with medieval history, English history and royal biography, it reveals how individual rulers, decisions and betrayals changed the course of a nation.
Perfect for viewers interested in Anglo-Saxon England, Viking history, medieval warfare, royal dynasties and the origins of the English crown, this film tells the complete story of England’s first dynasty: the Saxon kings of the House of Wessex.

snippet.title: How the Richest Man in Florida Built Palm Beach for a Woman 37 Years Younger and Died Alone
snippet.description:
In this in-depth, full-length documentary, we explore how Henry Morrison Flagler arrived in Ohio at fourteen years old with nine cents and a French five-franc coin in his pocket, became the silent operational genius behind John D. Rockefeller and Standard Oil, then walked away from the largest monopoly in American history in his fifties to invent Florida from scratch, built the Royal Poinciana and Whitehall in Palm Beach for his much younger second wife, engineered an Act of the Florida legislature so he could divorce his insane first wife and marry a woman thirty-seven years his junior, watched her abandon him for a violinist, and died after a fall in his palace at the age of 83 with the long codicil of a will that left almost nothing to his only surviving heir.

----------------------------------------

Gain FREE access to secret full-length documentaries on wealthy families "too scandalous for YouTube" by joining our newsletter: https://www.substack.com/@oldmoneyluxury

----------------------------------------

Henry Morrison Flagler was born on January 2, 1830, in Hopewell, New York, the son of a Presbyterian minister and a much-married mother whose previous unions had brought him a half-brother named Daniel M. Harkness and a step-half-brother named Stephen V. Harkness. The Harkness family had money. The Flagler family did not.

In 1844, age fourteen, he left home for Republic, Ohio, where the Harkness side of the family ran a country store. He arrived with nine cents and a French five-franc coin. Within twenty years he had bought into a Bellevue distillery, sold it during the Civil War, lost most of the proceeds to a failed salt venture in Saginaw, Michigan, and returned to Cleveland in 1866 essentially broke.

There he met John D. Rockefeller. Stephen V. Harkness, by then one of the richest men in Ohio, agreed to put $100,000 into the new oil refining business on the condition that Flagler be appointed treasurer and silent partner. The firm became Rockefeller, Andrews & Flagler in 1867 and was incorporated as Standard Oil in 1870.

Rockefeller called Flagler "the brains and judgment behind the entire enterprise." Flagler personally negotiated the secret railroad rebates and drawbacks that crushed Standard Oil's competitors through the South Improvement Company scheme of 1872 and the bigger rebate program that followed it. He drafted the trust agreement that made Standard Oil the first modern American holding company in 1882. By the time he turned his attention to Florida, his personal fortune was estimated at $60 million.

His first wife Mary Harkness, his step-half-brother's sister, had died of tuberculosis in 1881. His second marriage, in 1883, was to Ida Alice Shourds, an actress and Mary's former nurse. Ida Alice descended into florid psychosis through the 1890s, was committed to Choate Sanatorium in 1896, and was declared legally insane in 1898.

In 1899 Flagler took up with a thirty-four-year-old North Carolina widow named Mary Lily Kenan. He was sixty-nine. To marry her he engineered Senate Bill 132 through the Florida legislature in 1901, which made incurable insanity grounds for divorce, an Act that applied to no one else in Florida and that was repealed within a few years. He divorced Ida Alice and married Mary Lily on August 24, 1901.

Florida itself he had been building since 1885. He bought the Jacksonville, St. Augustine and Halifax River Railway and extended it down the east coast in a single straight line that became the Florida East Coast Railway. He built the Ponce de Léon Hotel in St. Augustine, then the Royal Poinciana in Palm Beach in 1894, the largest wooden building in the world. He built The Breakers next to it in 1896. For Mary Lily he built Whitehall, a 75-room beaux-arts marble palace finished in 1902 as her wedding present, at a cost of $4 million.

In 1912 he completed the Overseas Railroad to Key West, a 156-mile rail line across the open Atlantic, the most expensive single piece of railway construction in American history.

On January 15, 1913 he fell on the marble stairs at Whitehall. He died on May 20, 1913, age 83.

Mary Lily inherited the bulk of the estate, married a North Carolina state senator named Robert Bingham within four years, and died at Bingham's house in Louisville under circumstances that produced a midnight exhumation, a sealed pathologist's report, and the Bingham family newspaper dynasty in Kentucky. Henry Flagler's surviving son and only direct heir, Harry Harkness Flagler, received the use of a small trust and the active enmity of his father's executors.

The railroad to Key West was destroyed by the Labor Day Hurricane of 1935. The Royal Poinciana was demolished in 1934. Whitehall was nearly demolished in 1959 and saved at the last minute as the Flagler Museum.

Palm Beach is still there.

snippet.title: The Gilded Age Men Who Were Destroyed By The Women They Loved (Documentary)
snippet.description:
The Gilded Age Men Who Were Destroyed By The Women They Loved (Documentary)

@OldMoneyCorrupts

In eighteen seventy two, a three hundred pound showman bled to death on a hotel staircase, shot by the man who stole his mistress. In nineteen oh six, the most famous architect in America was executed at point blank range inside the very building he designed, murdered by the husband of a girl he had drugged and violated at sixteen. And in eighteen ninety, an heir to Alexander Hamilton's bloodline was found floating face down in a Wyoming river, destroyed by a woman he met in a brothel. Three fortunes. Three women. Three men who believed their money made them untouchable. Every one of them was wrong.
